sections.heading: The Seven Classical Planets
paragraphs: Ancient astrology is limited to the seven visible planetary bodies: the Sun, the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. These are the naked-eye wanderers. They are the only objects that a pre-telescopic observer could see moving against the fixed stars across human-scale timeframes, and they form the bedrock of every astrological tradition from Babylon onward.

Modern astrology added Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto after their telescopic discovery. Astra Antiqua receives them the way Rome received a foreign god: formally, under a native name, and on the record as an admission rather than a birthright. Every culture's deity table marks each of the three a received body and says in its own note that no ancient scribe ever tallied a planet for it. The reception is modern interpretive work, built by the same functional and iconographic method described below, and it is never presented as the ancients' own.

sections.heading: Interpretatio Graeca and Beyond
paragraphs: Ancient cultures systematically identified each other's gods. The Greeks called this practice the interpretatio graeca: Egyptian Thoth was identified with Hermes, Canaanite Baal with Zeus, Phoenician Melqart with Heracles, and so on. The Romans inherited and extended this method (interpretatio romana), and the Hellenistic and Imperial periods produced a dense overlay of cross-cultural identifications that show up in inscriptions, magical papyri, and astrological literature.

These identifications were not casual. They were grounded in functional resemblance (sky-god to sky-god, war-god to war-god), iconographic overlap (the cresent, the bull, the trident), and ritual analogy. The five-pantheon translation matrix in this app stands in the same tradition. Each planetary assignment is justified either by direct ancient testimony or by a defensible functional and iconographic argument, and the cases where the evidence is weaker are flagged below.

sections.heading: Our Translation Matrix
paragraphs: The ten planetary bodies in this app split into two groups. Seven archetypes are drawn from the Hellenistic tradition (chiefly Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos and Vettius Valens); three (Uranus, Neptune, Pluto) are modern receptions built by the same method and marked as such wherever they appear. The five cultural pantheons are then mapped onto all ten using primary sources where available for the seven: Ugaritic tablets for Canaan, Hellenistic astrological literature for Greece, Punic inscriptions and Imperial syncretisms for Carthage, Egyptian funerary and astronomical texts (with their later Greco-Egyptian recensions) for Egypt, and the Roman augural tradition with its Sibylline and interpretatio romana literature for Rome. For the three received bodies, no primary source exists by definition; the mapping is original interpretive work, done in the ancient manner and disclosed as such rather than dressed up as antiquity.

Some of these mappings are strong and well-attested. Others are reconstructive choices that prioritize legibility for a modern reader over strict philological caution. Those cases are listed in the next section.

notes.title: Saturn = Geb (Egypt)
notes.body: The Egyptian planetary name for Saturn was 'Horus Bull of the Sky.' We use Geb because his archetypal weight as the ancient earth-father better translates the Saturn principle for modern readers. This is an interpretive choice, not a hard historical identification.

notes.title: Tanit = Moon (Carthage)
notes.body: Tanit was a composite goddess. Iconography (the crescent over solar disc) and Greek syncretism with Artemis support her lunar identification, and she is conventionally classed as a lunar goddess. She also absorbed many functions of Astarte, the Phoenician Venus, and was identified with Juno Caelestis in Roman Africa. We assign her to the Moon because the iconography is most clear-cut there, and place Astarte at Venus.

notes.title: Mercury = Sebegu / Set (Egypt)
notes.body: The association of Mercury with Set is attested in later periods. Early Egyptian astronomy named the planet Sebegu without strong identification with a major god. Set's chaotic, swift nature became the predominant association in Greco-Egyptian syncretism.

notes.title: Baal Hammon at both Jupiter and Saturn (Carthage)
notes.body: Baal Hammon is the chief male deity of Carthage. The Romans equated him with Saturnus in his agricultural and time-keeping role (Saturnus Africanus), but his sky-sovereign aspect maps cleanly to Jupiter as well. Rather than force a single planetary assignment, we let the same deity occupy both seats, with two distinct epithets (Lord of the Sky for Jupiter, the Ancient One for Saturn) marking the functional difference. This dual placement is itself an interpretive choice and is flagged here.

sources.author: Frank Moore Cross
sources.title: Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic
sources.detail: Harvard University Press, 1973. Standard synthesis of Northwest Semitic religion and the divine council tradition.

sources.author: F. O. Hvidberg-Hansen
sources.title: La déesse TNT: Une étude sur la religion canaanéo-punique
sources.detail: G.E.C. Gad, 1979. Foundational study of Tanit and the Punic religious system.

sources.author: Dennis Pardee
sources.title: Ritual and Cult at Ugarit
sources.detail: Society of Biblical Literature, 2002. Critical translations of the Ugaritic ritual texts.

sources.author: Claudius Ptolemy
sources.title: Tetrabiblos
sources.detail: Second century CE. The classical formalization of Hellenistic astrology and the seven-planet system. Loeb edition (F. E. Robbins, translator) is standard.

sources.author: Vettius Valens
sources.title: Anthology
sources.detail: Second century CE. The most extensive surviving Hellenistic astrological compendium. Mark Riley's English translation is the accessible reference.

sources.author: Otto Neugebauer and Richard Parker
sources.title: Egyptian Astronomical Texts
sources.detail: Brown University Press, three volumes, 1960 to 1969. The standard corpus of Egyptian planetary, decanal, and ceiling-chart material.

sources.author: Roger Beck
sources.title: A Brief History of Ancient Astrology
sources.detail: Blackwell, 2007. Accessible scholarly overview of the Hellenistic synthesis and its sources.

sources.author: Astra Antiqua editorial
sources.title: The reception of Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto
sources.detail: Not sourced from any ancient text, because none exists. The three modern bodies are seated by the same functional and iconographic method described above (interpretatio romana), applied by this project's editors to bodies unknown before the eighteenth and twentieth centuries. Every placement carries a note beginning 'Received' rather than being presented as ancient testimony.
